claims.evidence: StatPearls Hand Bones excerpt: each hand consists of 27 bones; OpenStax gives eight carpals in wrist, five metacarpals in palm, 14 phalanges.
OpenStax: eight carpals in two rows of four; only scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum contribute to the radiocarpal joint, so 'with the radius' reworded.
claims.newSentence: The carpal bones lie in two rows of four, and only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum contribute to the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.

claims.evidence: OpenStax 8.2: 'The most commonly fractured carpal bone is the scaphoid, often resulting from a fall onto the hand'; 'typically' softened to 'often'.
claims.newSentence: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, often as a result of a fall onto the hand.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Hand Bones excerpt: 27 bones; StatPearls hand embryology and OpenStax give eight carpals, five metacarpals, 14 phalanges.
OpenStax: proximal row scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, listed lateral to medial; StatPearls Hand Carpal Bones lists radial to ulnar.
OpenStax: distal row trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate, listed lateral to medial; StatPearls Hand Carpal Bones gives the same order.
OpenStax: scaphoid and lunate meet the radius directly, but the triquetrum articulates with a fibrocartilaginous pad, so 'all three articulate with the radius' is incorrect.
claims.newSentence: Scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum contribute to the radiocarpal joint; the scaphoid and lunate articulate directly with the radius

claims.evidence: OpenStax: thumb has a proximal and a distal phalanx; digits two to five each have proximal, middle and distal phalanges.
StatPearls Wrist Flexor Retinaculum: forms anterior roof of carpal tunnel; contains 4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL tendon (nine) and the median nerve.
CUH: fractures sometimes not visible on first X-ray, repeat X-ray at clinic. Plymouth: repeat examination and X-ray, MRI if suspicion continues.
claims.newSentence: X-ray first; a scaphoid fracture does not always show at first, so a repeat X-ray or an MRI scan may follow

claims.evidence: OpenStax: wrist and base of hand have eight carpals; palm holds five metacarpals; thumb and fingers hold 14 phalanges.
OpenStax: metacarpals numbered 1 to 5 from the thumb side. 'Each associated with a group of phalanges' not found; clause dropped.
claims.newSentence: The metacarpals are numbered one to five starting from the thumb side.

claims.evidence: OpenStax chapter review and 8.2 summaries: first metacarpal freely mobile, moves independently; the rest function as one unit forming the palm.
claims.newSentence: The first metacarpal is freely mobile, moving independently of the others, which join together to make up the palm.

claims.evidence: OpenStax: thumb has a proximal and a distal phalanx; digits two to five each have proximal, middle and distal phalanges.
OpenStax: expanded distal end of each metacarpal articulates at the MCP joint with the proximal phalanx, and also forms the knuckles.
claims.newSentence: The expanded distal end of each metacarpal articulates with the proximal phalanx of the thumb or one of the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joint, and also forms the knuckles of the hand.

claims.evidence: OpenStax: eight carpals in a proximal row of four and a distal row of four; StatPearls: eight carpal bones divide into two rows.
OpenStax and StatPearls Hand Carpal Bones both list proximal and distal rows in this order, lateral (radial) to medial (ulnar).
OpenStax glosses: scaphoid boat-shaped, lunate moon-shaped, triquetrum three-cornered, pisiform pea-shaped, capitate head-shaped, hamate hooked bone.
OpenStax: pisiform projects anteriorly, forming a bony bump felt at the medial base of the hand; hamate has an anterior hook of the hamate.
OpenStax: only scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum contribute to radiocarpal joint; scaphoid and lunate meet radius directly, triquetrum a fibrocartilaginous pad.
claims.newSentence: Only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum contribute to the radiocarpal joint: the scaphoid and lunate articulate directly with the distal end of the radius, whereas the triquetrum articulates with a fibrocartilaginous pad.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Wrist Flexor Retinaculum: fibrous connective tissue band forming anterior roof of carpal tunnel; many experts treat it as synonymous with transverse carpal ligament.
claims.newSentence: The flexor retinaculum is a fibrous connective tissue band that forms the anterior roof of the carpal tunnel at the wrist, and many experts consider it synonymous with the transverse carpal ligament.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: posterior to the flexor retinaculum, in the tunnel, are 4 FDS tendons, 4 FDP tendons, the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the median nerve.
claims.newSentence: Posterior to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel, lie the four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, the four flexor digitorum profundus tendons, the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the median nerve.

claims.evidence: Gateshead: pressure on the median nerve as it passes through the wrist. NCBI review: pain, numbness, tingling in the median nerve distribution.
NCBI review excerpt (Genova et al., PMC7164699): weakness, clumsiness and eventual atrophy of the thenar muscles as the disease advances.
claims.newSentence: As the condition advances there can be weakness and eventual wasting of the thenar muscles at the base of the thumb.

claims.evidence: Ligament thickening and tendon swelling not found on cited pages. StatPearls CTS: raised tunnel pressure is the primary factor; Gateshead: cause unknown in most cases.
claims.newSentence: Raised pressure within the carpal tunnel is the primary factor in the onset of the condition, although in most cases the underlying cause is unknown.

claims.evidence: OpenStax: scaphoid is most commonly fractured carpal bone. CUH says 'small hand bone', Plymouth 'thumb side of the wrist'; 'base of the thumb' not stated.
claims.newSentence: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, and NHS trust leaflets describe it as a small bone of the hand on the thumb side of the wrist.

claims.evidence: CUH and Plymouth: scaphoid fractures usually follow a fall onto an outstretched hand; Royal Cornwall and Gloucestershire say the same for wrist fractures.
claims.newSentence: Scaphoid fractures and wrist fractures usually result from a fall onto an outstretched hand.

claims.evidence: CUH: pain and tenderness just below base of thumb. Plymouth: pain, tenderness or swelling; most scaphoid fractures leave wrist looking normal with mild symptoms.
claims.newSentence: A scaphoid injury typically causes pain and tenderness near the base of the thumb, and the wrist may swell, but most scaphoid fractures leave the wrist looking normal and cause only mild symptoms.

claims.evidence: Plymouth lists trouble gripping or twisting the wrist or thumb among symptoms. CUH does not mention it.
Gloucestershire distal radial fracture page: immediate severe pain, swelling, often deformity, painful movement, sometimes tingling or numbness. Royal Cornwall lists none of these.
claims.newSentence: One NHS trust page on distal radial fractures, which are breaks of the forearm bone next to the wrist joint, describes immediate severe pain, swelling and often deformity of the wrist, painful movement, and sometimes tingling or numbness in the fingers.

claims.evidence: Royal Cornwall: wrist fractures are common in young children and older people. Gloucestershire names different groups, so it is not cited for this.
No retrieved CUH or Plymouth text says a sprain mimics a scaphoid fracture or that suspected injuries prove to be sprains or bruises.
'Stable fracture' and 'thin crack' wording not found at CUH or Plymouth; the retrievable point (not always visible on first X-ray) is kept in c34.
CUH: fractures sometimes, but not always, show up straight away on X-ray. Plymouth: a fracture can take days to appear on X-ray.
claims.newSentence: A scaphoid fracture does not always show on the first X-ray, and in some people it is not obvious until some days after the injury.

claims.evidence: Plymouth: return to fracture clinic for repeat examination and X-ray; MRI requested if suspicion continues. CUH: clinic repeat X-ray.
claims.newSentence: If the first X-ray does not show a fracture but one is still suspected, the person is examined again and the X-ray repeated at the fracture clinic, and an MRI scan is requested if suspicion continues.

claims.evidence: Plymouth: because the scaphoid has a poor blood supply, staff assume the bone is broken until this is ruled out; described as the safest option.
claims.newSentence: One NHS trust leaflet explains that, until a fracture can be ruled out, the wrist is treated as if the bone were broken, because the scaphoid has a poor blood supply.

claims.evidence: Northampton: X-ray produces images of the inside of the body, quick and painless; hold still during exposure; more than one X-ray from different angles.
claims.newSentence: An X-ray is a quick, painless procedure that produces images of the inside of the body. The person needs to keep still during the exposure so the picture is not blurred, and more than one X-ray may be taken from different angles.

notes: Convention: 'unsupported'+'edited' means one clause could not be confirmed and was cut, and only the confirmed remainder (or the retrieved statement on the same point) was kept. 1) Wrong: draft said scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum all articulate with the radius (c02, c07, c20); OpenStax says the triquetrum meets a fibrocartilaginous pad, so wording corrected. 2) Carpal tunnel syndrome: PMC7164699 itself was never returned verbatim; symptoms and thenar wasting came from the excerpt of that review (Genova et al.) and NCBI summaries, and the URL appeared in link lists, so please eyeball c23-c25. Ligament thickening and tendon swelling (c25) were not found on any cited page; replaced with the StatPearls CTS statement that raised tunnel pressure is the primary factor, plus Gateshead's 'cause unknown in most cases'. StatPearls CTS (NBK448179) was added as a reference for that. 3) NHS leaflet attribution: Cambridge says 'small hand bone' and lists only pain and tenderness (no swelling or grip difficulty); Plymouth alone lists swelling and trouble gripping or twisting, and 'most fractures leave the wrist looking normal with mild symptoms'. Royal Cornwall does not mention the scaphoid or the c30 symptom list; c30 rests on Gloucestershire alone, now attributed to 'one NHS trust page'. Gloucestershire names different at-risk groups, so c31 rests on Royal Cornwall only. Neither Cambridge nor Plymouth text showed 'stable fracture', 'thin crack', 'sprain' or 'bone bruise' (c32, c33 removed). Plymouth's 80 per cent detection figure and the 10 to 14 day interval were deliberately not carried into prose (CLINICAL.md 5.5). 4) c13: OpenStax summaries disagree on wording ('united' versus 'fused', neither a quote); sentence reworded to the shared meaning, so check the exact OpenStax phrase if desired. 5) c09 'nine' is the sum of the listed tendons (4+4+1); one StatPearls entry also states nine flexor tendons. 6) No sentence needed the 'textbook' class; the phrase 'at the base of the thumb' glossing the thenar muscles (c24) is the writer's definitional gloss. 7) Word count rose because corrections carry retrieved qualifiers (radius/pad nuance, single-page attribution); no new topics. Key-fact words 84 to 93. 8) structures unchanged (12 names, all in the atlas); they cover the right hand's carpals, first and fifth metacarpals and the two thumb phalanges only, which is an atlas limit, not something the article claims. 9) 26 of 30 searches used, all standard mode with one publisher domain each; none refused. Support came from search summaries, not page text, so the OpenStax and leaflet paraphrases are the main residual risk.
